one_line: Give exactly what the question asks for, in the number of items it asks for. Give the correct technical term or a precise fact. Do not copy words from the question. Do not explain unless the question also says describe or explain.

points.text: Short-answer questions usually give one mark for each correct item ('One from', 'Four from'). Some questions say 'identify and describe', or ask for an item and a description. For these, the mark scheme can use matched pairs. You get one mark for the item and one mark for a description that goes with it.

cites.quote: ONE from: • a cryptographic hash of the previous block • a timestamp • (all the) transaction data
Eight available. Max two for each matched pair: • Table name/title (1st)
Max FOUR marks, TWO per paired answer • Length check (1st)

points.text: For Identify, State and Name, a single word or short term can be enough. Examiners described one Identify question as looking for four one-word answers. Another question wanted only the name or acronym of a protocol. But when the question asks you to describe, one-word answers are not enough.

cites.quote: In effect, this question was a test of memory recall, as whilst the answer did not require precise wording, it was looking for four one-word answers
This question required only a name or acronym of a protocol that works at the internet layer.
As candidates were asked to describe, rather than state, answers needed to be more than one-word answers.

points.text: Give exactly the number of answers that the question asks for. The November 2023 examiner report says that examiners mark only the first answers, up to that number. Extra answers earn nothing.

cites.quote: Where candidates are asked for a specific number of answers, only the first of these up to that number will be marked. Therefore, for this question, if a candidate gave more than four answers, only the first four were marked.

points.text: Do not copy something from the question as your answer. If the question already names an item or gives an example, repeating it earns nothing. A new wording of the question also earns nothing, for example 'a command line interface uses commands'.

cites.quote: Candidates should not repeat the question in their answers. For example, Question 5(a) asks for one ‘other item of data’ but a significant number of candidates included the items given in the question stem in their answer, which did not gain them credit.
repetition of the theft of data, which was included in the question as an example, was not accepted.

For example, candidates stated that a command line interface used commands or a gesture-based interface used gestures. In cases where candidates answered in these terms, without any further expansion, no credit could be awarded.
some candidates stated that the age of information meant that information was outdated, which was not accepted, as it was effectively, a repeat of the question.

points.text: A definition must be precise. Examiners praised short, exact definitions such as 'a sequence of characters'. They called nearly-right answers a common mistake. One example is saying that encrypted data is unreadable. In fact the data is readable, but its meaning is hidden. Learn the exact meaning of each syllabus term.

cites.quote: Many candidates could give the precise definition of a string as a ‘sequence of characters’.
One common mistake is considering that encrypted data is unreadable without a key, which is one advantage of encrypting the data.
Many candidates could not precisely define a virtual currency and muddled their answers with vague details of different forms of digital currency
This question assessed candidates’ ability to provide definitions of key terms from the syllabus.

points.text: Use the exact names from the syllabus. Made-up names such as 'updating maintenance' got no marks. Be as specific as the question asks. For example, 'numeric' was not enough when the question asked which numeric data type.

cites.quote: Poorer answers incorrectly named the maintenance as e.g., ‘updating maintenance’ or ‘replacement’ maintenance. The names of the types of maintenance are given in Topic 16.8 so candidates are reminded to use these.
Typical issues included stating that the field was numeric, but not stating what type of numeric field was best, or simply confusing the data types.

points.text: Answer the actual question. If it asks you to give reasons, a description gets no marks. If it asks how something could go wrong, a definition gets no marks.

cites.quote: Many candidates described tunnelling which did not answer the question. The question required candidates to give reasons why it would be used.
Candidates who failed to achieve marks usually did so because they gave a definition of visual checking, rather than answer the question.

points.text: Short answers must still fit the scenario. Examiners did not accept answers about the wrong part of the scenario.

cites.quote: Where candidates did not achieve full marks, this was often because they listed issues to do with the train service itself.
When faced with a question that has a clear context, learners should take this as an opportunity to apply their understanding in the particular context.

points.text: Suggest is rare, with 2 parts from 2022 onward. One of them has an examiner comment. That question was about improving a flowchart. The suggestions had to be relevant, and each one had to fit clearly on the flowchart. A 2021 report on a Suggest question criticised answers that said what something was. Those answers did not give reasons that fitted the scenario.

cites.quote: As the question asks for improvement to the flowchart, candidates had to ensure that suggested improvements were both relevant and able to be clearly placed on the flowchart.
While many responses provided some detail about what incremental prototyping involved, most did not give reasons why it might be used when developing a spreadsheet for managing finances.

question.quote: Identify four factors which can affect the quality of information.

examples.note: The mark scheme accepts Accuracy, Relevance, Age, Level of detail and Completeness, one mark each. Four correct words get all four marks. The examiner report says the question was looking for four one-word answers. Write only four, because examiners do not mark extra answers.

question.quote: Blockchains contain the records and the cryptographic hashes used to secure the records. State one other item of data that makes up the blockchain.

earns.quote: ONE from: • a cryptographic hash of the previous block • a timestamp

weak.answer: The cryptographic hashes that secure the records.
weak.why: The question already gives this item. Repeating the question stem earns nothing.

basis.quote: a significant number of candidates included the items given in the question stem in their answer, which did not gain them credit.

examples.note: Before you answer, read the stem and cross out anything it already gives. 'Other' means something that is not in the question.

question.quote: JavaScript can manipulate and store strings in variables. (a) Define the term string as used in JavaScript.

strong.sentence: A string is a sequence of characters.

earns.quote: (An object representing) a sequence of (any) characters.

examples.note: One short, precise sentence gets the mark. The examiner report says that good answers gave the precise definition 'sequence of characters'.

thin_evidence: Counts from the question papers, from 2022 onward: Identify 28, State 12, Give 11, Define 8, List 2, Suggest 2, Name 1. The two List parts also ask you to describe. The one Name part (March 2026, Paper 12 Q10) actually says 'identify'. The Suggest advice rests on only one question from 2022 onward with an examiner comment (9626_w23_qp_13 Q8), plus one 2021 report. So treat that advice as thin. Give, Name and List are not in the syllabus command-word table. We found no examiner report that says whether an example in a definition gains or loses marks. So this section makes no claim about it.
